brief.head: Vulgar familiarity
brief.text: A fi­nance man may find bank­ing reg­u­la­tion easy and mon­e­tary pol­icy mys­te­ri­ous, Ajay Shah said. Familiarity says noth­ing about dif­fi­culty; shared met­rics pro­tect against it. {101-C06}

brief.head: Float first
brief.text: Monetary pol­icy is easy only when prop­erly struc­tured, Ajay Shah said: an in­fla­tion tar­get, a well-composed com­mit­tee, a float­ing ex­change rate and an open cap­i­tal ac­count. {#float}

brief.head: No mythological beast
brief.text: It all starts at pub­lic choice the­ory, Ajay Shah said: “The gov­ern­ment is not a mytho­log­i­cal crea­ture of in­fi­nite ca­pa­bil­ity. The gov­ern­ment is a deeply flawed crea­ture.” {101-C01}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on what the state can do
lead.head: Four tests before the state acts

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 101

body: Amit Varma opened the episode in the dark. “I don’t know if you can see us,” he said, and turned the gloom into a para­ble about the state: in­ter­ven­tion was meant to light the way, “but in­stead it burnt ev­ery­thing to the ground and there is no power any­more.” {101-J01}

He was, he ad­mit­ted, being a lit­tle over-dramatic. The episode, part of the hosts’ se­ries on the state, asked a sober ques­tion. When some­one de­mands that the gov­ern­ment act, can it ac­tu­ally suc­ceed?
Ajay Shah’s an­swer is that this ques­tion must come first. Implementation con­straints, he said, be­long on the table right at the start of any pol­icy dis­cus­sion. {101-C02}

Mainstream Indian de­bate, he said, “blithely runs for­ward” from val­ues to ac­tion. Judge first what is easy and what is hard, and scarce money and man­age­ment ef­fort can be ra­tioned: some lovely ob­jec­tives let go, the winnable ones taken on.
## The tool­kit
The tool­kit grew out of work by Lant Pritchett and Michael Woolcock, which Shah and Vijay Kelkar ex­tended. It asks four ques­tions of any pro­posed in­ter­ven­tion.
How many trans­ac­tions does it in­volve? How much dis­cre­tion do the front­line work­ers have? How high are the stakes? How opaque is the work?

The higher each one scores, the harder the job. Five hun­dred re­search grants a year are easy to man­age; polio drops for 500 mil­lion peo­ple are not. A po­lice­man who can jail you holds high stakes; a vac­ci­na­tor holds none.
Once learnt, Shah said, the tool­kit fits in your head, ready for any hos­tel-room de­bate on in­fla­tion tar­get­ing. {101-C03}
Varma no­ticed that all four tests probe the same gap, be­tween what the state wants and what its em­ploy­ees want.
## Scoring the state

Shah’s chief demon­stra­tion is cen­tral bank­ing. Monetary pol­icy, prop­erly struc­tured around an in­fla­tion tar­get, is easy: a com­mit­tee of five makes six de­ci­sions a year, in pub­lic. Financial reg­u­la­tion is hard, and al­ways will be.
Then the hosts built a table on the fly. Elementary schools scored two out of four. A vac­ci­na­tion drive was easy. The ju­di­ciary scored three and a half.
Taxation, with high trans­ac­tions, high dis­cre­tion, stakes of thou­sands of crores and com­plete opac­ity, was “four on four”. {101-C04}

A hard row is not the end, Shah ar­gued. Monetary pol­icy was once opaque and ruled by a pow­er­ful gov­er­nor; an in­fla­tion tar­get, a com­mit­tee and full trans­parency hacked it into an easy prob­lem. Good IT sys­tems can do the same by strip­ping dis­cre­tion from clerks.
## Smith’s short list
The deep­est im­pli­ca­tion came with Adam Smith, who said lit­tle else is needed for a state’s op­u­lence but peace, easy taxes and a tol­er­a­ble ad­min­is­tra­tion of jus­tice.

Run those through the four tests, Shah said, and all three are bru­tally hard. The min­i­mal state, it turns out, is not an easy state, which is why he would refuse every dis­trac­tion from that core. {101-C07}
Varma added a cau­tion. The met­rics mea­sure how hard a job is, not how much it mat­ters, and Smith’s three must be done how­ever hard they are.
The dan­ger, he said, is the drunk who searches for his key under the lamp­post, not be­cause he dropped it there but be­cause that is where the light is.
Too many, he wor­ried, set­tle for “easy prob­lems that are in­con­se­quen­tial and don’t re­ally move the nee­dle”.

second.label: Central banking
second.head: Easy money, hard banks
second.deck: Why Ajay Shah calls monetary policy trivial and financial regulation four on four

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on monetary policy and financial regulation

body: We tend to see cen­tral bank­ing as one blur, Ajay Shah said. The day he saw it as two jobs, one easy and one hard, was one of the happy days of his life. {101-R05}

A mod­ern mon­e­tary pol­icy com­mit­tee should have five mem­bers: the RBI gov­er­nor and four in­de­pen­dent pri­vate econ­o­mists. They meet six times a year to hit a 4 per cent in­fla­tion tar­get, and each writes down why they voted. {101-S02} “Six trans­ac­tions a year. That’s it,” Shah said. “For the rest in the year you’re sleep­ing.”

Financial reg­u­la­tion is the op­po­site: a thou­sand firms, some 2,000 touch points a year, judg­ment calls on whether a loan is an NPA, bil­lions of dol­lars at stake and su­per­vi­sion in se­crecy. {#touchpoints}

quote.text: So for all the hype and mys­tique around mon­e­tary pol­icy, ac­tu­ally it’s a triv­ial, easy prob­lem.

third.head: No one was saved

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the exit ramps from hard work

body: The state’s real work, Ajay Shah said, is peace, easy taxes and a tol­er­a­ble ad­min­is­tra­tion of jus­tice. But these things are hard, so ev­ery­body takes some exit ramp or other.
He counts two ramps. The first is wel­fareism: hu­man­i­tar­ian projects that bring the sat­is­fac­tion of hav­ing fed some chil­dren lunch, with­out solv­ing the hard prob­lems. {#ramps}

The sec­ond is unique to en­gi­neers: build an IT sys­tem. Riffing on P. Sainath’s book *Everybody Loves a Good Drought*, Shah and Vijay Kelkar ti­tled a sec­tion of *In Service of the Republic* “Everybody Loves a Good IT System”. {101-J11}

“Some soft­ware ven­dor builds an app, some soft­ware ven­dor builds a web­site, you cel­e­brate, you’ll in­au­gu­rate it, noth­ing will get done,” Shah said. {101-C10} His ver­dict came from the Beatles’ *Eleanor Rigby*: “No one was saved.” {101-J09}

p2.title: Easy or hard?
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s four tests of feasibility, argued over with Amit Varma, chapter by chapter

from1.head: Four tests before the state acts

quote.text: We should al­ways bring im­ple­men­ta­tion con­straints on the table. Like right up front, start think­ing, can we do it?

box.title: The paper behind the toolkit
box.text: Ajay Shah loves *Solutions When the Solution is the Problem* be­cause the ques­tion it asked, whether an in­ter­ven­tion is easy or hard to im­ple­ment, was it­self a break­through. Lant Pritchett and Michael Woolcock wrote it in 2004, propos­ing the first two tests. {#origin}

sections.label: The question
sections.head: First ask: can it be done?
sections.caption: asking whether it can be done
body: Amit Varma framed the ques­tion. Whether the state should in­ter­vene, he said, de­pends not only on whether the in­ter­ven­tion is jus­ti­fied, but on whether it is pos­si­ble: whether it will work, and how hard or easy it is.
Ajay Shah went fur­ther. Implementation con­straints, he ar­gued, should come up front in every dis­cus­sion of pub­lic pol­icy. {101-C02}

The hosts’ scep­ti­cism has deep roots, and Shah re­stated four of them. The world is too com­plex, so the true facts about a so­ci­ety are un­know­able to plan­ners. {#unknowable} The in­cen­tives of the state’s per­son­nel clash with its ob­jec­tives. Special in­ter­est groups kick the gov­ern­ment around. And even well-meant projects are badly im­ple­mented.
Hence, he said, the “en­vi­ron­ment of dif­fi­dence” the hosts bring when­ever some­one says the gov­ern­ment will do one new thing.
## A judg­ment in a flash

Shah’s test case was mil­i­tary. Landings in Burma and in China are both very hard, but any­one can see at once that the first is pos­si­ble and the sec­ond prac­ti­cally im­pos­si­ble. The aim is to make such calls rou­tine for pol­icy. {101-S01}
Mainstream Indian pol­icy, he said, rarely asks the ques­tion at all. Yet judg­ing what is easy and what is hard is what lets a gov­ern­ment ra­tion its money and man­age­ment ef­fort.
~ Some lovely ob­jec­tives, he said, should sim­ply be let go: “We won’t be able to win this one.”

quote.text: We should al­ways bring im­ple­men­ta­tion con­straints on the table. Like right up front, start think­ing, can we do it?

sections.label: The four tests
sections.head: What makes a job hard
sections.caption: the four tests of difficulty
body: Faced with any prob­lem, from uni­ver­sal small­pox vac­ci­na­tion to mak­ing the po­lice work, Ajay Shah ap­plies four tests. The higher a job scores on each, the harder it is.
The first is the num­ber of trans­ac­tions. A gov­ern­ment might put out 500 re­search grants a year, he said, while polio vac­ci­na­tion means touch­ing 500 mil­lion peo­ple. {#polio}

The sec­ond is the dis­cre­tion of front­line work­ers. “We are all deeply wired to be kind to our friends and fam­ily and our kids and kin,” Shah said, so dis­cre­tion is often used against the organisation’s ob­jec­tives.
These two came from Lant Pritchett and Michael Woolcock. Vijay Kelkar and Shah added the other two.
## Stakes and se­crecy
A po­lice­man who can put you in jail is in a high-stakes con­ver­sa­tion with you. Someone giv­ing a child polio drops has noth­ing to gain: low stakes.

Then opac­ity. Body cams, pub­lished sta­tis­tics, the CAG and RTI let jour­nal­ists, re­searchers and op­po­si­tion par­ties kick up a fuss. Without them, Shah said, “like any­thing can be done”. {#rti}
~ Amit Varma saw one thread run­ning through all four: the gap be­tween the ob­jec­tives of the state and the in­cen­tives of its em­ploy­ees. {#thread}

quote.text: We have a clear tool­kit and you don’t even need paper and pen. You can just mem­o­rise this.

sections.label: Worked examples
sections.head: Six calls a year, or 2,000
sections.caption: monetary policy and taxation
body: Asked by Amit Varma to show, not tell, Ajay Shah began with an op-ed whose title says it all: *Monetary policy is easy; Financial regulation is hard*. {101-R05}

A prop­erly struc­tured mon­e­tary pol­icy com­mit­tee makes six de­ci­sions a year to hit a 4 per cent in­fla­tion tar­get, and each mem­ber writes down why. Low trans­ac­tions, low dis­cre­tion, low stakes, no se­crecy.

Financial reg­u­la­tion is four on four: a thou­sand firms, about 2,000 touch points a year, judg­ment calls on bad loans, bil­lions of dol­lars at stake, and su­per­vi­sion done in se­cret. {#touchpoints}
## Filling in the table

Varma then imag­ined a table and called out rows. Elementary schools have high trans­ac­tions, and teach­ers with com­plete dis­cre­tion over whether to teach, make eye con­tact or try three times harder. But a teacher’s wage is mod­est, so stakes are low, and opac­ity can be fixed. Two out of four.
A vac­ci­na­tion cam­paign, for HPV or polio, fol­lows a fixed pro­to­col, and the vac­ci­na­tor has noth­ing to gain: easy. {#hpv}
The ju­di­ciary has ul­ti­mate dis­cre­tion and ul­ti­mate stakes, and judges on a bench de­lib­er­ate be­hind closed doors: three and a half out of four. {#judiciary}
~ Taxation, which Varma called Shah’s favourite sub­ject, was the worst: thou­sands of crores at stake for big ac­counts, and com­plete opac­ity. Four on four. {101-C04}

quote.text: High num­ber of trans­ac­tions, high dis­cre­tion in the hands of the tax of­fi­cer, high stakes, sky high stakes

sections.label: The hacker’s turn
sections.head: Hard problems, hacked
sections.caption: redesigning hard into easy
body: Amit Varma, sure that Ajay Shah is a hacker at heart, asked whether the table it­self could be hacked.
It could, Shah said. Stare at a bad row and ask whether the pol­icy can be re­designed to turn a hard prob­lem into an easy one.

Modern mon­e­tary pol­icy is the proof. It was once messy and opaque, run by a pow­er­ful gov­er­nor who could do what­ever they wanted. An in­fla­tion tar­get, a com­mit­tee dom­i­nated by pri­vate econ­o­mists and com­plete trans­parency hacked its com­po­nents. {101-C05}
## The ticket win­dow

Information tech­nol­ogy can do the same, Shah ar­gued in a 2005 paper on IT in gov­er­nance. {#itpaper} High trans­ac­tions are mostly about pieces of paper: mov­ing them be­tween of­fices, guard­ing them against coun­ter­feits. Computerise them, and the prob­lem can go away.

Discretion can be tamed too. When train book­ings lived in a paper reg­is­ter, the clerk at the ticket win­dow could say there was no seat. {101-S03} In an open data­base, seat 2A is ei­ther taken or not.
~ That, Shah said, is the real value of an IT sys­tem: it re­moves dis­cre­tion from the front­line civil ser­vant and con­verts a com­po­nent from hard to easy.

quote.text: So we changed our whole par­a­digm of how to think about this in order to make it easy.

sections.label: The hardest basics
sections.head: Three basics, a century’s work
sections.caption: Adam Smith’s three essentials
body: Amit Varma brought in Francis Fukuyama’s dis­tinc­tion be­tween a state’s scope, how many things it does, and its strength, how well it does them. India’s state is high on scope and low on strength. Is that be­cause the few things it must do well are hard? {101-C09}

Ajay Shah an­swered with what he called one of the great­est quotes in eco­nom­ics. Adam Smith wrote that lit­tle else is needed to carry a state from the low­est bar­barism to the high­est op­u­lence but “peace, easy taxes, and a tol­er­a­ble ad­min­is­tra­tion of jus­tice”. {101-J10}
## No easy min­i­mal state

Run those through the four tests, Shah said, and every one is very hard. Peace means the mil­i­tary, the po­lice, crim­i­nal jus­tice and courts. Taxation and the ju­di­ciary al­ready sat at the top of the table.

State ca­pa­bil­ity has a bud­get con­straint, he ar­gued: money, the head­count of civil ser­vants and, above all, the at­ten­tion of lead­ers, re­searchers and re­form­ers. Getting the core right could take 50 to 100 years, so every other cal­en­dar entry should get a no. {#century}
~ Varma added that hard is not the same as unim­por­tant. Smith’s three are nec­es­sary and prac­ti­cally suf­fi­cient, so they must be done how­ever hard they are. {101-C08}

quote.text: both you and I agree that what the Indian State should do is it should do a few things well, not many things badly
the met­rics that we laid out are not met­rics for im­por­tance, they’re met­rics for how hard some­thing is. And just be­cause some­thing is very hard doesn’t mean that it should not be done.

p3.title: Parables of the state
p3.deck: A drunk, a ticket clerk, Nehru in 1947 and an imagined landing

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s parable, and his charge against RCTs
stories.head: The key is in the dark
body: One night, a drunk man is search­ing under a lamp­post. A po­lice­man comes up, and Amit Varma was par­tic­u­lar about him: “a good po­lice­man in a coun­try with rule of law”. {101-J08}

“My friend, what are you look­ing for? Can I help you?” the po­lice­man asks. The drunk man is look­ing for his key, so the po­lice­man, “with great hu­mil­ity and a sense of ser­vice”, helps him look.
They search for some time and find noth­ing. At last the po­lice­man asks where the key was dropped. “Over there in the bushes where it’s very dark,” says the drunk man.
Then why look here? “Because this is where the light is.”
Varma’s worry is that many of us go after easy prob­lems that are in­con­se­quen­tial and do not move the nee­dle, rather than solv­ing the hard ones.

He used the same para­ble to open his *The Seen and the Unseen* episode with Lant Pritchett, aimed at RCTs in de­vel­op­ment eco­nom­ics. “RCTs are solv­ing in­con­se­quen­tial, easy prob­lems sim­ply be­cause they’re at­trib­ut­able and mea­sur­able,” he said, “and it’s a great fraud on the field of eco­nom­ics.” {101-S05}
The tough prob­lems are dif­fi­cult and fuzzy, Varma said, “and that’s what a real man tries to solve and Lant Pritchett is a real man”.

~ Later Varma found that the scholar Yuen Yuen Ang had used the same metaphor, al­most si­mul­ta­ne­ously, in her paper *Adaptive Political Economy*. He wrote to her, and says she will be on his show once she fin­ishes a very im­por­tant book. {101-J15}
stories.why: Measurable, at­trib­ut­able prob­lems tempt us be­cause they let us feel pro­duc­tive, while the prob­lems that mat­ter stay fuzzy and in the dark. It is worth ask­ing whether you work on some­thing be­cause it mat­ters or be­cause it is well lit.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the drunk under the lamppost

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the railway register and the lying clerk
stories.head: Seat 2A, taken or not?
body: In the olden days, Ajay Shah said, the book­ing sta­tus of every seat on every train was kept on paper, in a reg­is­ter in­side the rail­way of­fice. {101-S03}
So the clerk at the ticket win­dow had com­plete dis­cre­tion. “He could lie to you,” Shah said. “He could say there’s no ticket here.”

Then the book­ings went into a data­base open to the whole world, ide­ally through an API, and the dis­cre­tion was gone. “It’s black and white,” Shah said. “Seat num­ber two A, is it taken? Is it not taken?”
~ The gov­ern­ment need not even run IRCTC, he added. It only has to open up an API, and ClearTrip and MakeMyTrip will do the rest. {#api}
stories.why: The real value of a good IT sys­tem, Shah said, is that it strips dis­cre­tion from the front­line civil ser­vant, and so turns a hard com­po­nent into an easy one.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the railway ticket clerk

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah imagines a different conversation in 1947
stories.head: Hands full, Mr Nehru
body: Imagine, Ajay Shah said, that in 1947 some­body told Jawaharlal Nehru to work on peace, easy taxes and a tol­er­a­ble ad­min­is­tra­tion of jus­tice, Adam Smith’s three es­sen­tials. {101-S04}
In Shah’s telling, Nehru brushes it off: yes, yes, that is all good, but we also need land re­form.

The right an­swer, Shah ar­gued, would have been alarm: “Wow, peace very hard. Easy taxes, very hard. Tolerable ad­min­is­tra­tion of jus­tice, very hard. We have our hands full, we are swamped. Don’t give me any­thing more to do.”
~ Every extra project, he said, drains money, civil ser­vants and the at­ten­tion of lead­ers from a core that could take 50 to 100 years to get right. {#century}

quote.text: Our con­clu­sion should be that it is very hard to do these ba­sics. So don’t do mis­sion creep.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on what Nehru should have heard

stories.head: Burma yes, China no
body: Picture a hy­po­thet­i­cal Indian ex­pe­di­tionary force, Ajay Shah said, weigh­ing land­ings in Burma against land­ings in China. {101-S01}

In a flash, we know the an­swer. Both are very hard. But push comes to shove, a suf­fi­ciently com­plex Indian naval op­er­a­tion could land troops in Burma, while land­ings in China are prac­ti­cally im­pos­si­ble.
“Watch what we just did,” Shah said. “We dis­cussed a prob­lem state­ment and we ar­rived at a judg­ment that is this easy or is this hard.”

~ Could the same quick call be made about the clam­our of de­mands on the state: to ma­nip­u­late the ex­change rate, sta­bilise in­fla­tion, build an atom bomb or run polio vac­ci­na­tion? “Amazingly enough,” Shah said, “the an­swer is yes.” {#yes}
stories.why: We al­ready judge fea­si­bil­ity at a glance in some fields. The four tests make that move rou­tine for pol­icy, so that pro­pos­als are weighed on whether they can work, not just on whether they are de­sir­able.

quiz.q: Which four tests does Ajay Shah apply to judge how hard a state intervention is?
quiz.a: Transactions, front­line dis­cre­tion, stakes and opac­ity: the higher each scores, the harder the job.

quiz.q: How many decisions a year must a modern monetary policy committee get right?
quiz.a: Six, which is why Shah calls mon­e­tary pol­icy a triv­ial, easy prob­lem.

quiz.q: Which job did Shah score “four on four”, with stakes of thousands of crores?
quiz.a: Taxation: high trans­ac­tions, high dis­cre­tion, sky-high stakes and com­plete opac­ity.

quiz.q: What were Adam Smith’s three requirements for carrying a state from barbarism to opulence?
quiz.a: Peace, easy taxes and a tol­er­a­ble ad­min­is­tra­tion of jus­tice, each very hard.

quiz.q: Why could the old railway ticket clerk tell you there were no seats?
quiz.a: Bookings sat in a paper reg­is­ter, giv­ing him com­plete dis­cre­tion to lie.

quiz.q: In Amit Varma’s parable, why does the drunk search under the lamppost?
quiz.a: Because that is where the light is, though the key fell else­where.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 101. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Adam Smith (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Francis Fukuyama (Gobierno de Chile, CC BY 2.0); Leonard Cohen (Rama, CC BY-SA 2.0 fr); Van Morrison (Art Siegel (artolog on flickr), CC BY-SA 2.0).

shelf.title: Solutions When the Solution is the Problem: Arraying the Disarray in Development
shelf.creator: Lant Pritchett and Michael Woolcock
shelf.why: Pritchett and Woolcock ask whether an in­ter­ven­tion is easy or hard to im­ple­ment, a ques­tion Ajay calls a break­through that Indian pol­icy de­bate rarely asks: in­ter­ven­tions with many trans­ac­tions or much dis­cre­tion for front­line staff are harder to de­liver.

shelf.title: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (Episode 379, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A deep con­ver­sa­tion with Lant Pritchett on why growth, not re­dis­tri­bu­tion, drives human wel­fare, why causal­ity runs from de­vel­op­ment to ed­u­ca­tion, and why many RCTs solve small mea­sur­able prob­lems in­stead of mov­ing the nee­dle on poverty.

shelf.title: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (Episode 402, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A ten-and-a-half-hour con­ver­sa­tion with Ajay about his life and ideas, in­clud­ing the in­side story of how India built a good eq­uity mar­ket through SEBI, NSE and NSDL.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: Monetary policy is easy; Financial regulation is hard
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It is the orig­i­nal state­ment of the episode’s cen­tral worked ex­am­ple: two ‘cen­tral bank’ jobs that dif­fer sharply in dif­fi­culty.

shelf.title: Improving governance using large IT systems
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It ar­gues that IT can tame high-transaction, high-discretion com­po­nents and make a hard prob­lem man­age­able.

shelf.title: How to correctly draw the perimeter for government software systems (Big Ideas, Episode 20)
shelf.why: It ex­pands on the idea that the state should open up an API and let pri­vate play­ers like ClearTrip and MakeMyTrip build on it.

shelf.title: Adaptive Political Economy: Toward a New Paradigm
shelf.creator: Yuen Yuen Ang
shelf.why: He calls it a fan­tas­tic paper by a great scholar who reached the same di­ag­no­sis on her own.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything’s series on the state (Episodes 25, 26, 33, 91, 92, 99)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The foun­da­tion of the show’s think­ing on gov­ern­ment: the state is a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence that acts through co­er­cion, so every in­ter­ven­tion, paid for by taxes, must be jus­ti­fied.

shelf.title: Don’t Mess With the Exchange Rate (Episode 67, EIE)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why the ex­change rate is the most im­por­tant price in the econ­omy and should be set by the mar­ket: rig­ging it to make ex­porters look com­pet­i­tive is a trans­fer from the poor, and man­ag­ing it in­vites cur­rency crises.

shelf.title: Rethinking Innovation Policy (Episode 59, EIE)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why re­search fund­ing in India is ‘a truly bad space’, and the al­ter­na­tive: an in­dus­try-neutral ap­proach that con­tracts R&D out through grants to uni­ver­si­ties and pri­vate firms rather than hav­ing bu­reau­crats pick sec­tors.

shelf.title: Eleanor Rigby
shelf.creator: The Beatles
shelf.why: A beau­ti­ful song that, for Ajay, cap­tures how he thinks about most gov­ern­ment IT sys­tems.

shelf.title: Bad
shelf.creator: U2
shelf.why: One of two songs from that album he calls ‘ab­so­lutely great’.

shelf.title: Promenade
shelf.creator: U2
shelf.why: The sec­ond of his two picks from the album.

shelf.title: No Surprises
shelf.creator: Radiohead
shelf.why: He loves the orig­i­nal as much as the cover, which he calls ‘one of those schiz­o­phrenic things in my head’.

shelf.title: No Surprises (cover)
shelf.creator: Regina Spektor
shelf.why: He calls it a beau­ti­ful cover he ab­so­lutely loves, on a par with the orig­i­nal.

shelf.title: Suzanne
shelf.creator: Leonard Cohen
shelf.why: A ‘re­ally, re­ally deep song’ and ‘one of the great songs to know’.

shelf.title: Aubrey
shelf.creator: Bread
shelf.why: He wants to bring at­ten­tion back to a for­got­ten band’s song.

shelf.title: Bhatiali Dhun
shelf.creator: Jaya Bose and Himangshu Biswas
shelf.why: He first thought it was nos­tal­gia, but after all these years de­cided ‘it’s not mere nos­tal­gia, it’s some­thing truly cool’.

shelf.title: Madame George
shelf.creator: Van Morrison
shelf.why: One of Amit’s favourite songs of all time, ‘an ab­so­lutely epic’ song and the cen­tre­piece of Astral Weeks, an album he con­sid­ers a mas­ter­piece.

shelf.title: Madame George (cover)
shelf.creator: Marianne Faithfull
shelf.why: ‘A glo­ri­ous ethe­real cover’ of Van Morrison’s Madame George, one of the two great ver­sions Amit rec­om­mends along­side the orig­i­nal.

shelf.title: Madame George (cover)
shelf.creator: Luka Bloom
shelf.why: Another fan­tas­tic ver­sion of Van Morrison’s Madame George, by the Irish singer-songwriter Luka Bloom.

shelf.title: Paper Thin Hotel
shelf.creator: Greg Dulli
shelf.why: He calls it ‘an ab­so­lute masterpiece’.

laughs.text: Amit opens in the dark (‘I don’t know if you can see us’) and turns it into a para­ble: ‘We are shrouded in dark­ness today. The light of free­dom has gone out of our lives. Everyone thought in­ter­ven­tion will show us a way... but in­stead it burnt ev­ery­thing to the ground and there is no power any­more.’

After Ajay says Lant Pritchett would agree that their ex­tended ver­sion is bet­ter, Amit plugs his Seen and the Unseen episodes. Ajay now has four­teen, ‘tied with our good friend Pranay Kotasthane... it’s a good bat­tle who’s gonna win.’
Amit on Ajay’s aca­demic stan­dards: ‘I told you, hey, don’t bring your pa­per­wala goals to the show... So I’m very happy for you, fi­nally an episode with novel in­sights.’
Amit uses the writ­ing-workshop rule on Ajay to ask for ex­am­ples: ‘I’m gonna do the writer thing and tell you now. Don’t tell me, show me, show, don’t tell.’
Ajay’s teacher-discretion ex­am­ple asks ‘Do I teach to the ge­nius Amit Varma in my front row...?’ Amit protests: ‘I was al­ways a back­bencher... I never sat on a front bench.’
Amit, de­lighted with the dif­fi­culty table: ‘I want you to build ta­bles like this for me in every area of my life, so all my de­ci­sion mak­ing be­comes easy.’

In the lamp­post para­ble Amit stresses this is ‘a good po­lice­man in a coun­try with rule of law’ who helps ‘with great hu­mil­ity and a sense of service’. He also de­clares that the tough, fuzzy prob­lems are ‘what a real man tries to solve and Lant Pritchett is a real man.’
Ajay on gov­ern­ment IT launches: ‘you cel­e­brate, you’ll in­au­gu­rate it, noth­ing will get done... No one was saved. Eleanor Rigby.’ Amit signs off: ‘We’ve got a Beatles song about IT sys­tems.’

Adam Smith, which Ajay calls one of the great­est quotes in eco­nom­ics: ‘lit­tle else is req­ui­site to carry a state to the high­est de­gree of op­u­lence from the low­est bar­barism, but peace, easy taxes, and a tol­er­a­ble ad­min­is­tra­tion of jus­tice. All the rest being brought about by the nat­u­ral course of things.’
P. Sainath’s book ‘Everybody Loves a Good Drought’, which Kelkar and Shah riff on in a sec­tion ti­tled ‘Everybody Loves a Good IT System’.
Francis Fukuyama’s dis­tinc­tion be­tween the scope of a state (how many things it does) and its strength (how well it does them).
Jawaharlal Nehru in 1947, imag­ined brush­ing off Smith’s three es­sen­tials in favour of land re­form.

Transparency in­sti­tu­tions as checks on the state: ‘just imag­ine if there was no CAG, if there was no RTI... then like any­thing can be done.’ Also the Indian Financial Code drafted by FSLRC, cited as the kind of prop­erly drafted law that makes in­fla­tion tar­get­ing easy to roll out.

Yuen Yuen Ang’s ‘Adaptive Political Economy’ uses the same drunk-under-the-lamppost metaphor that Amit used to open his Lant Pritchett episode. Amit says she will be on The Seen and the Unseen once she fin­ishes a very im­por­tant book she is writ­ing.
